How it declined or fell # Four Anglo-Mysore Wars; Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, and the British restored the Wodeyars as subordinate rulers. Legacy # Rocketry and Mysore Dasara.

d: A private company ruled India with its own army of ~260,000.
x: Overview # A private company ruled India with its own army of ~260,000. Government and society # A joint-stock company governed by directors in London, supervised from 1773 by Parliament, ruled through a Governor-General in Calcutta and presidencies in Madras and Bombay, with a private army of Indian sepoys. How people lived # Peasants paid high land revenue; weavers lost markets to British cloth. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Company paintings and early printing presses in Calcutta. Food # Indians ate traditional grains and pulses, but Company revenue demands contributed to famines such as the Bengal famine of 1770, which killed about a third of the province’s people. Construction and architecture # Fort William in Calcutta, Fort St George in Madras and neo-classical government buildings. Technology and knowledge # Surveys such as the Great Trigonometrical Survey (from 1802), which later measured Everest; steamships and the first telegraph lines. How it rose # Victory at Plassey (1757) and the diwani of Bengal (1765) turned the Company into a territorial power; wars against Mysore, the Marathas and Sikhs extended its rule. How it declined or fell # The 1857 uprising led Parliament to abolish Company rule in 1858. Legacy # Colonial administration, the drain of wealth, and the deindustrialisation of Indian textiles.

d: Ended with Independence and Partition in 1947.
x: Overview # Ended with Independence and Partition in 1947. Government and society # India was ruled by a Viceroy responsible to the Secretary of State in London; about 1,000 Indian Civil Service officers governed 300 million people. About 560 princely states remained under indirect rule. Limited reforms (1909, 1919, 1935) gave Indians some elected seats. How people lived # Most Indians remained farmers facing famines; cities grew with mills, railways and an English-educated middle class. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Bengal Renaissance, new Indian newspapers, and the rise of nationalism. Food # Most Indians ate rice or wheat, pulses and vegetables; famines in 1876–78, 1896–1902 and 1943 killed tens of millions while grain was exported. Construction and architecture # New Delhi by Lutyens and Baker, Indo-Saracenic buildings such as Victoria Terminus (Mumbai) and the Victoria Memorial (Kolkata), hill stations and cantonments. Technology and knowledge # About 67,000 km of railways, telegraph, canals in Punjab, and the census; but designed largely to serve British commercial and military needs. How it rose # After 1857 the British Crown took direct control (1858); Victoria became Empress of India in 1877. How it declined or fell # The mass freedom movement led by Gandhi, Nehru, Bose, Patel and many others, the 1946 naval mutiny, Britain’s exhaustion after WWII, and the end of Indian soldiers’ loyalty led to independence and Partition on 15 August 1947. Legacy # Parliamentary institutions, English as a link language and railways, but also famines, poverty, communal division and Partition.

d: The earliest Chinese writing on oracle bones.
x: Overview # The earliest Chinese writing on oracle bones. Government and society # Shang kings ruled with the help of ancestors, consulted through divination; they led armies, performed sacrifices (including human sacrifice) and controlled bronze production. How people lived # Millet farmers, bronze casters and diviners lived around royal centres. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Ancestor worship and oracle-bone divination. Food # Millet in the north and rice in the south, plus pigs, dogs and fermented alcoholic drinks made in bronze vessels. Construction and architecture # The capital Yin (Anyang) had rammed-earth palace foundations and royal tombs; Erlitou (possibly Xia) had the earliest palaces in China. Technology and knowledge # Sophisticated bronze casting with piece-moulds, horse-drawn chariots, silk and the oracle-bone script, ancestor of Chinese characters. How it rose # The Shang overthrew the semi-legendary Xia around 1600 BCE according to tradition. How it declined or fell # The last Shang king, remembered as a tyrant, was defeated by the Zhou around 1046 BCE. Legacy # Writing, bronze art and ancestor veneration that shaped Chinese civilisation.

d: China's longest dynasty.
x: Overview # China’s longest dynasty. Government and society # The Western Zhou kings granted land to relatives and allies in a feudal system, justified by the Mandate of Heaven: heaven grants the right to rule to the virtuous and withdraws it from tyrants. After 771 BCE royal power faded and states competed in the Spring and Autumn (770–476) and Warring States (475–221) periods. How people lived # Peasants worked land for lords under a feudal order. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Confucian rites, the Book of Songs and Taoist ideas. Food # Millet, wheat, soybeans, vegetables and meat for nobles; elaborate ritual banquets were described in the Book of Rites. Construction and architecture # Walled cities, ancestral temples and elaborate ritual bronze vessels with long inscriptions. Technology and knowledge # Iron tools and casting, the crossbow, cavalry, and large irrigation works such as Dujiangyan (256 BCE), still in use. How it rose # King Wu of Zhou defeated the last Shang king at Muye around 1046 BCE. How it declined or fell # Nomad attacks and rebellion forced the move east in 771 BCE; afterwards the Zhou kings were figureheads until Qin extinguished them in 256 BCE. Legacy # Confucius, Laozi, Mencius and Sunzi lived in the Zhou era, the classical age of Chinese philosophy.

d: Gave China its name.
x: Overview # Gave China its name. Government and society # Qin Shi Huang ruled by Legalist principles: strict laws, harsh punishments, collective responsibility, and abolition of feudal fiefs in favour of 36 commanderies run by appointed officials. How people lived # Peasants were conscripted for armies and huge building projects. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Standardised writing and legalist philosophy. Food # Millet and wheat, with state granaries feeding armies. Construction and architecture # The emperor’s tomb near Xi’an, guarded by about 8,000 life-size terracotta soldiers, horses and chariots; the first connected Great Wall; and the vast Epang Palace. Technology and knowledge # The Qin standardised script, coins, weights, measures and axle widths, built about 6,800 km of roads and the Lingqu canal linking the Yangtze and Pearl river systems, and mass-produced crossbows with interchangeable parts. How it rose # Qin, a western state, became powerful after Shang Yang’s Legalist reforms (4th century BCE). King Ying Zheng conquered the other six Warring States by 221 BCE and named himself First Emperor. How it declined or fell # Massive forced labour, harsh laws and book burning provoked hatred. After the First Emperor died in 210 BCE, the Chen Sheng–Wu Guang uprising and other rebellions brought down the dynasty by 206 BCE. Legacy # The name ‘China’ probably comes from Qin; the unified written language and centralised state lasted two millennia.

d: Han is still the name of China's majority people.
x: Overview # Han is still the name of China’s majority people. Government and society # The Han combined Qin centralisation with Confucian ideals. Emperor Wu (r. 141–87 BCE) made Confucianism the state ideology and founded an Imperial Academy; officials were recommended for virtue and tested on the classics. Commanderies and counties were run by appointed officials, with state monopolies on salt and iron to raise revenue. How people lived # Peasant families farmed with iron ploughs; officials studied Confucian classics. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Silk, lacquer, paper and the historian Sima Qian. Food # Millet, wheat (as noodles), rice, soybeans and tofu (traditionally Han), plus pork and tea. Construction and architecture # Han cities such as Chang’an and Luoyang had walled palaces and markets; tombs held clay models of houses, watchtowers and farms showing everyday buildings. The Han extended the Great Wall west into the Gansu corridor to protect Silk Road trade. Technology and knowledge # Cai Lun refined papermaking around 105 CE; Zhang Heng built a seismoscope (132 CE) and a water-powered armillary sphere; the Han also developed the wheelbarrow, blast furnaces producing cast iron, the rudder, the horse collar and acupuncture texts. How it rose # Liu Bang, a peasant-born official, rebelled after the Qin collapse and defeated the aristocrat Xiang Yu in 202 BCE, founding the Han. He softened Qin’s harsh laws while keeping its centralised structure. How it declined or fell # Land concentration, court intrigue between eunuchs and consort families, and natural disasters led to the Yellow Turban rebellion (184 CE). Warlords who suppressed it carved up China; in 220 the last Han emperor abdicated, beginning the Three Kingdoms. Legacy # The Han defined Chinese identity; the majority ethnic group still calls itself Han. Paper, the Silk Road and the Confucian civil service were its lasting gifts.

d: A golden age of Chinese culture.
x: Overview # A golden age of Chinese culture. Government and society # The Tang emperor ruled through the Three Departments and Six Ministries: a Secretariat drafted edicts, a Chancellery reviewed them, and the Department of State Affairs carried them out through ministries of personnel, revenue, rites, war, justice and works. Officials were increasingly chosen by competitive imperial examinations on the Confucian classics and poetry. The ‘equal-field’ system allotted land to peasant households in return for taxes in grain and cloth and labour service, and the Tang Code (624) became the model for law across East Asia. Wu Zetian (r. 690–705) became China’s only woman emperor in her own name. How people lived # Chang’an was a cosmopolitan city of about a million. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Poetry of Li Bai and Du Fu, tea culture and Buddhist art. Food # Rice, wheat cakes, mutton and tea, which became a national drink; foreign foods such as grapes and sesame cakes were popular in Chang’an. Construction and architecture # Chang’an, the capital, was the largest city in the world (~1 million people), laid out on a strict grid of 108 walled wards around a central avenue 150 m wide, with two great markets where Persians, Sogdians, Arabs and Indians traded. The Tang built the Giant Wild Goose Pagoda to house sutras brought from India by Xuanzang, the vast Daming Palace, Buddhist cave temples at Longmen and Dunhuang, and wooden halls that influenced Japanese temples like those of Nara. Technology and knowledge # The Tang produced the world’s oldest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra (868), by woodblock printing; early porcelain and sancai three-colour glazed ceramics; mechanical clocks with water-driven escapements; advances in medicine (Sun Simiao’s encyclopaedias), cartography and astronomy (Yi Xing measured the meridian). Alchemists experimenting with saltpetre and sulphur took the first steps toward gunpowder. How it rose # After the short Sui dynasty reunified China (581) but exhausted it with huge canal projects and failed wars in Korea, rebellions broke out. Li Yuan, a Sui general, and his son Li Shimin captured Chang’an and founded the Tang in 618. Li Shimin, as Emperor Taizong (r. 626–649), defeated the Eastern Turks, extended control along the Silk Road into Central Asia, and governed so effectively his reign became a byword for good rule. How it declined or fell # In 751 the Tang lost to the Abbasids at the Battle of Talas, ending expansion westward. In 755 the general An Lushan rebelled; the eight-year An Lushan rebellion devastated the north and may have cost millions of lives. Afterwards provincial military governors (jiedushi) became semi-independent, eunuchs dominated the court, and the equal-field system collapsed. The Huang Chao rebellion (874–884) sacked Chang’an, and in 907 the warlord Zhu Wen deposed the last Tang emperor, opening the Five Dynasties period. Legacy # The

d: The world's most advanced economy of its time.
x: Overview # The world’s most advanced economy of its time. Government and society # The Song placed civilian scholar-officials above generals, recruiting them through greatly expanded examinations. Reformers like Wang Anshi tried state loans to farmers and new taxes; Neo-Confucian thinkers like Zhu Xi reshaped education. How people lived # Commercial towns, rice farmers and scholar-officials. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Landscape painting, printed books and the tea house. Food # Champa rice, tea, restaurants and teahouses in cities; the first known restaurant menus. Construction and architecture # Song builders wrote the Yingzao Fashi construction manual (1103), built tall pagodas and covered bridges, and laid out bustling commercial cities like Kaifeng, shown in the scroll ‘Along the River During the Qingming Festival’. Technology and knowledge # The Song had the world’s most advanced economy: gunpowder weapons and fire lances, the magnetic compass for navigation, movable type (Bi Sheng, ~1040), the first government paper money (jiaozi), large ocean-going junks with watertight bulkheads, and new rice varieties from Champa that doubled harvests. How it rose # General Zhao Kuangyin was proclaimed emperor by his troops in 960 and reunified most of China, ending the Five Dynasties chaos. How it declined or fell # The Song lost the north to the Jurchen Jin in 1127 and moved its capital to Hangzhou. The Mongols conquered the Jin, then besieged Song cities for decades; the last Song emperor died at the naval Battle of Yamen in 1279. Legacy # Printing, the compass and gunpowder spread from Song China to the world; Song landscape painting and porcelain set lasting standards.

d: Founded by Genghis Khan's grandson.
x: Overview # Founded by Genghis Khan’s grandson. Government and society # Kublai Khan ruled China as Great Khan and Emperor, dividing society into four ranks: Mongols, Semu (Central Asians and others), northern Chinese and southern Chinese. The examination system was suspended until 1315 and many officials were foreigners, among them Persians, Uyghurs and, by his own account, Marco Polo. How people lived # Mongol, Chinese and foreign populations under a layered order. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Yuan drama and blue-and-white porcelain. Food # Mongol mutton, dairy and soups combined with Chinese rice dishes. Construction and architecture # The new capital Dadu (Khanbaliq, today’s Beijing) was laid out on a classical grid with palaces, lakes and the White Pagoda, built by the Nepali architect Araniko. Technology and knowledge # Paper money circulated empire-wide. The Grand Canal was extended to Beijing. Guo Shoujing built observatories and calculated the year to within 26 seconds. Postal relay stations (yam) linked China to Persia. How it rose # Genghis Khan’s Mongols attacked the Jin from 1211. His grandson Kublai declared the Yuan dynasty in 1271 and destroyed the Southern Song in 1279, the first time a non-Chinese people ruled all of China. How it declined or fell # Failed invasions of Japan (1274, 1281) and Java drained the treasury, and paper-money inflation and Yellow River floods followed. Plague and ethnic discrimination fuelled the Red Turban revolts. Zhu Yuanzhang took Dadu in 1368 and the Mongols withdrew to the steppe. Legacy # It reunified China after centuries of division and opened the age of Silk Road contact with Europe described by Marco Polo. It also produced zaju drama.

d: Rebuilt the Great Wall in stone.
x: Overview # Rebuilt the Great Wall in stone. Government and society # The founding emperor Hongwu abolished the post of chancellor and ruled personally through ministries, with a secret police (the Embroidered Uniform Guard). Later emperors relied heavily on eunuchs. The examination system and the eight-legged essay dominated elite life. How people lived # A large farming population and busy market towns. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Porcelain, Ming novels and the Forbidden City. Food # Rice and new American crops: maize, sweet potatoes and chillies. Construction and architecture # The Ming built the Forbidden City in Beijing (1406–1420), the Temple of Heaven, the Ming tombs and rebuilt the Great Wall in brick and stone into the form seen today. Technology and knowledge # Zheng He’s treasure fleets (1405–1433) sailed ships far larger than European vessels to India, Arabia and East Africa. The Ming produced famous blue-and-white porcelain, encyclopaedias like the Yongle Encyclopedia, and adopted New World crops such as maize and sweet potatoes. How it rose # Zhu Yuanzhang, a peasant orphan and former monk, led the Red Turban rebellion against the Mongol Yuan and founded the Ming in 1368. How it declined or fell # Bureaucratic paralysis, eunuch corruption, costly wars in Korea against Japan, silver shortages, Little Ice Age famines and epidemics led to peasant revolts. Rebel Li Zicheng took Beijing in 1644; the last emperor hanged himself, and the Manchus swept in as the Qing. Legacy # The Forbidden City, the Great Wall in its famous form, porcelain trade with the world and classic novels like Journey to the West.

d: China's last imperial dynasty.
x: Overview # China’s last imperial dynasty. Government and society # The Manchu Qing ruled with a dual Manchu–Han bureaucracy and the Eight Banners military system. Emperors Kangxi, Yongzheng and Qianlong (1661–1796) presided over a long era of prosperity and territorial expansion into Tibet, Xinjiang and Mongolia. How people lived # A population boom to about 400 million farmers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Peking opera and Qing literature. Food # Rice, maize and the Manchu–Han imperial feast. Construction and architecture # The Qing expanded the Summer Palace and Old Summer Palace (destroyed by British and French troops in 1860), and the Potala-style temples at Chengde. Technology and knowledge # Qing China adopted Jesuit astronomy and cartography, but by the 19th century fell behind Europe’s industrial technology. How it rose # The Manchus, unified by Nurhaci, took Beijing in 1644 after the Ming collapse. How it declined or fell # Population pressure, corruption, the Opium Wars (1839–42, 1856–60), the Taiping Rebellion (1850–64) and other revolts, unequal treaties, defeat by Japan (1895), and the Boxer Rebellion (1900) undermined the dynasty. The 1911 Xinhai Revolution ended over 2,000 years of imperial rule. Legacy # Modern China’s borders largely reflect Qing conquests.

d: Silla's capital Gyeongju had an observatory (Cheomseongdae).
x: Overview # Silla’s capital Gyeongju had an observatory (Cheomseongdae). Government and society # In the Three Kingdoms period, Goguryeo, Baekje and Silla were monarchies ruled with powerful aristocracies. Silla used the ‘bone-rank’ system: birth into ‘sacred bone’ or ‘true bone’ lineages decided who could hold office. How people lived # Farmers and aristocratic elites. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Buddhist temples such as Bulguksa. Food # Rice, barley and fermented vegetables. Construction and architecture # Goguryeo left painted tombs and mountain fortresses. Baekje’s Mireuksa temple pagoda and Silla’s capital Gyeongju (Cheomseongdae observatory, Bulguksa temple, Seokguram grotto) survive. Technology and knowledge # Silla’s Cheomseongdae (7th century) is among the oldest surviving observatories in East Asia. Baekje transmitted writing, Buddhism and craftsmen to Japan. All three produced superb gold crowns and metalwork. How it rose # The kingdoms took shape from the 1st century BCE to the 4th century CE. Goguryeo grew to rule much of Manchuria under Gwanggaeto the Great (r. 391–413). How it declined or fell # Silla allied with Tang China to conquer Baekje (660) and Goguryeo (668), then expelled the Tang by 676 to unify most of the peninsula. Unified Silla later split amid noble revolts and gave way to Goryeo in 935. Legacy # The first unification of Korea, Korean Buddhist art and the transmission of continental culture to Japan.

d: King Sejong created Hangul.
x: Overview # King Sejong created Hangul. Government and society # Joseon was a Neo-Confucian monarchy run by scholar-officials (yangban) chosen by civil service examinations. Royal records (the Annals of the Joseon Dynasty) were kept with such independence that even kings could not read them. How people lived # Confucian society of yangban, farmers and artisans. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Hangul, pansori and kimchi culture. Food # Rice, kimchi (chilli was added in the 18th century) and many banchan side dishes. Construction and architecture # Gyeongbokgung and Changdeokgung palaces in Seoul, Jongmyo royal shrine and the Hwaseong fortress at Suwon. Technology and knowledge # King Sejong (r. 1418–1450) commissioned Hangul (1443), a phonetic alphabet designed so ordinary people could read. His scholars also built rain gauges, water clocks and sundials. Admiral Yi Sun-sin’s ironclad ‘turtle ships’ defeated Japanese fleets in the 1590s. How it rose # General Yi Seong-gye overthrew the Goryeo dynasty in 1392 and moved the capital to Hanyang (Seoul). How it declined or fell # Japanese (1592–98) and Manchu (1627, 1636) invasions devastated the country. Factional strife and isolation as the ‘Hermit Kingdom’ followed. Japan forced open its ports (1876), made Korea a protectorate in 1905 and annexed it in 1910. Legacy # Hangul, Confucian family culture and one of the world’s longest-ruling dynasties (518 years).

d: The world's first novel by Murasaki Shikibu.
x: Overview # The world’s first novel by Murasaki Shikibu. Government and society # The emperor reigned in Heian-kyō (Kyoto), but real power passed to the Fujiwara clan, who ruled as regents by marrying daughters into the imperial family. Later, retired emperors ruled ‘from the cloister’ (insei). How people lived # Aristocrats in Kyoto; peasants farmed rice. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Tale of Genji and waka poetry. Food # Rice, fish and vegetables; Buddhism discouraged meat. Construction and architecture # Kyoto was laid out on a grid modelled on Chang’an. Byōdō-in’s Phoenix Hall and shinden-style aristocratic mansions with gardens and ponds also survive. Technology and knowledge # The kana syllabaries developed, letting writers, many of them court women, write Japanese phonetically. How it rose # Emperor Kanmu moved the capital to Heian-kyō in 794 to escape the power of Nara’s Buddhist monasteries. How it declined or fell # Provincial warrior clans grew strong. The Genpei War (1180–85) between the Taira and Minamoto ended with Minamoto no Yoritomo founding the Kamakura shogunate in 1185. Legacy # Murasaki Shikibu’s The Tale of Genji (~1010), often called the world’s first novel, and Sei Shōnagon’s Pillow Book.

d: Edo became one of the largest cities.
x: Overview # Edo became one of the largest cities. Government and society # The shogun ruled from Edo, while about 260 daimyo governed their domains. The ‘alternate attendance’ system (sankin-kōtai) made daimyo spend every other year in Edo and leave families there as hostages. Society was ranked as samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. How people lived # Samurai, farmers, artisans and merchants. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Kabuki, haiku (Bashō) and ukiyo-e prints. Food # Rice, miso, tofu; sushi and tempura stalls in Edo. Construction and architecture # Edo Castle, Himeji Castle (completed 1609), Nikkō’s Tōshō-gū shrine and merchant townhouses. Technology and knowledge # Japan was largely closed to foreigners (sakoku) except the Dutch at Dejima, through whom ‘Dutch learning’ (rangaku) brought European medicine and science. Literacy was high and woodblock printing (ukiyo-e) became a mass art. How it rose # Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara (1600) and became shogun in 1603, ending a century of civil war. How it declined or fell # Commodore Perry’s US ships (1853) forced Japan open. Unequal treaties and domestic unrest followed, and samurai from Satsuma and Chōshū overthrew the shogunate in the Meiji Restoration (1868). Legacy # Two and a half centuries of peace, haiku (Bashō), kabuki, Hokusai’s woodblock prints and the foundations of modern Japan.

d: An early Southeast Asian state.
x: Overview # An early Southeast Asian state. Government and society # Funan, known from Chinese records, was ruled by kings, said to descend from the marriage of an Indian Brahmin named Kaundinya and a local queen named Soma. How people lived # Farmers and port traders. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Hindu and Buddhist worship. Food # Rice from the Mekong delta and fish. Construction and architecture # Óc Eo, its port in the Mekong delta, had canals linking it to inland cities, brick buildings and workshops. Technology and knowledge # Canals for drainage and transport. Roman, Indian and Chinese goods have been found at Óc Eo. How it rose # It grew from about the 1st century CE as a stop on the sea route between India and China. How it declined or fell # Shifts in shipping routes through the Strait of Malacca weakened it, and by the 7th century Chenla had absorbed it. Legacy # The earliest Indianised state of mainland Southeast Asia.

d: Studied by Chinese pilgrim Yijing.
x: Overview # Studied by Chinese pilgrim Yijing. Government and society # A thalassocracy: maharajas at Palembang controlled the Strait of Malacca and Sunda Strait through allied ports and the loyalty of sea peoples (orang laut). How people lived # Sailors and traders around Palembang. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Buddhist learning centres. Food # Rice, sago, fish and spices. Construction and architecture # Little survives at Palembang. Related monuments include Muara Takus and, in Java, the Sailendra dynasty’s Borobudur. Technology and knowledge # Navigation with monsoon winds and control of shipping and taxes on the China–India sea trade. How it rose # Srivijaya emerged around 650 CE in Sumatra. The Chinese monk Yijing (671) found over a thousand monks studying there. How it declined or fell # The Chola king Rajendra I raided its ports in 1025. Later, Javanese Singhasari and Majapahit took over its role. Legacy # A major centre of Buddhist learning; Old Malay inscriptions are the ancestors of Malay and Indonesian.

d: Angkor may have been the largest pre-industrial city.
x: Overview # Angkor may have been the largest pre-industrial city. Government and society # The god-king (devaraja) cult linked the Khmer king to Shiva or Vishnu. The king ruled a vast network of provinces through officials and temple foundations. How people lived # Rice farmers supporting temple cities. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Apsara dance and Angkor’s reliefs. Food # Rice, fish (prahok paste) and fruit. Construction and architecture # Angkor Wat (early 12th century, built by Suryavarman II) is the largest religious monument in the world. Angkor Thom, the faces of the Bayon, and Ta Prohm (built by Jayavarman VII) also survive. Technology and knowledge # A huge hydraulic system of barays (reservoirs), canals and moats. Lidar shows Angkor was a sprawling low-density city of perhaps 750,000–900,000 people. How it rose # Jayavarman II declared independence from Java and himself universal monarch in 802 at Phnom Kulen. How it declined or fell # Overstretched water infrastructure, alternating mega-droughts and floods in the 14th–15th centuries, a shift to Theravada Buddhism and maritime trade, and attacks by Ayutthaya (1431) led the capital to move south. Legacy # Angkor Wat is on Cambodia’s flag. Khmer architecture influenced all of mainland Southeast Asia.

d: Inspired Indonesian nationalism.
x: Overview # Inspired Indonesian nationalism. Government and society # Kings ruled from Trowulan in East Java with powerful ministers, most famously Gajah Mada, who swore the Palapa oath not to rest until the archipelago was united. How people lived # Farmers and traders across Java. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Wayang shadow puppetry and Old Javanese poetry. Food # Rice, spices and coconut. Construction and architecture # Red-brick temples (candi) and gates such as Bajang Ratu, with the canals of Trowulan. Technology and knowledge # Rice irrigation, a large fleet and the spice trade. How it rose # Raden Wijaya used a Mongol invasion force to defeat his rival in 1293, then drove the Mongols out. How it declined or fell # Succession wars, the rise of Muslim port states such as Demak and Malacca, and Demak’s conquest around 1527. Legacy # A symbol of Indonesian unity; the Nagarakretagama poem. Bali preserves its Hindu culture.

d: Spread across the largest area of any pre-modern culture.
x: Overview # Spread across the largest area of any pre-modern culture. Government and society # Chiefs (ariki) of ranked lineages, tracing descent from gods and founding canoe voyagers, led island societies. Hawai’i and Tonga developed paramount kingships. How people lived # Settled Hawaii, New Zealand, Easter Island Culture, beliefs and heritage # Tattooing, navigation lore and oral genealogies. Food # Voyagers carried ‘canoe plants’ — taro, breadfruit, yam, banana, sugarcane, coconut and later sweet potato — plus pigs, dogs and chickens. Fish and shellfish provided protein. Construction and architecture # Marae temples, Tonga’s Ha’amonga trilithon, Rapa Nui’s moai statues and Hawai’i’s heiau and fishponds. Technology and knowledge # Double-hulled voyaging canoes navigated without instruments, using star paths, ocean swells, birds and clouds. The Hōkūleʻa voyages since 1976 proved such journeys possible. How it rose # Lapita ancestors reached Tonga and Samoa by about 800 BCE. Their descendants settled East Polynesia, Hawai’i, Rapa Nui and finally Aotearoa (~1250 CE). How it declined or fell # European contact from the 18th century brought diseases that killed many, missionaries, plantations and colonial annexation. Legacy # The most widespread human migration before modern times, across a third of the globe’s surface.

d: Weakened by the Thera eruption.
x: Overview # Weakened by the Thera eruption. Government and society # Palace centres such as Knossos, Phaistos and Malia redistributed goods and organised religion. Rulers may have been priest-kings or queens, and frescoes show women prominently. How people lived # Farmers, sailors and palace craftsmen. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Bull-leaping frescoes. Food # Olives, wine, honey, barley, legumes and fish; storage jars (pithoi) filled palace magazines. Construction and architecture # The palace of Knossos had multi-storey wings around a central court, light wells, painted plaster and flush drainage. Technology and knowledge # Linear A script (still undeciphered), sophisticated ships and fine pottery such as Kamares ware. How it rose # Bronze Age Cretan farming and sea trade grew into palace societies around 2000 BCE. How it declined or fell # The Thera (Santorini) eruption around 1600 BCE weakened them; by about 1450 BCE Mycenaean Greeks controlled Knossos. Legacy # Europe’s first palace civilisation; myths of the Minotaur and labyrinth.

d: Fell in the Bronze Age collapse.
x: Overview # Fell in the Bronze Age collapse. Government and society # Warrior kings (wanax) ruled palace states such as Mycenae, Pylos and Thebes, with scribes recording goods in Linear B, an early form of Greek. How people lived # Palace economies of farmers and warriors. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Gold masks and epic oral tradition. Food # Barley, wheat, olive oil, figs and wine; Linear B tablets record rations. Construction and architecture # Mycenae’s Lion Gate, Cyclopean walls and the beehive tholos tomb called the Treasury of Atreus. Technology and knowledge # Bronze armour (the Dendra panoply), chariots and Linear B. How it rose # Mainland Greeks absorbed Minoan culture from about 1600 BCE. How it declined or fell # The palaces were destroyed around 1200 BCE in the Bronze Age collapse. Causes probably combined drought, earthquakes, raiders and systems failure. Legacy # The world of Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey.

d: Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Parthenon.
x: Overview # Socrates, Plato, Aristotle, the Parthenon. Government and society # Hundreds of city-states (poleis) had different constitutions. Athens built a direct democracy in which citizen men voted in the Assembly and juries were chosen by lot after Cleisthenes’ reforms (508 BCE). Sparta was a militarised oligarchy with two kings. How people lived # Citizen farmers, artisans and enslaved workers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Theatre, the Olympics and philosophy. Food # Bread or barley porridge, olives, cheese, figs and wine mixed with water; meat came mainly from sacrifices. Spartans ate a notorious black broth. Construction and architecture # The Parthenon (447–432 BCE) with its Doric columns, theatres such as Epidaurus, and the agora and stoa. Technology and knowledge # Mathematics (Pythagoras, Euclid), medicine (Hippocrates), the trireme warship, and the Antikythera mechanism (later Hellenistic). How it rose # After the Greek Dark Ages, city-states revived from the 8th century BCE with the alphabet, colonies and the Olympic Games (776 BCE). They defeated Persia at Marathon (490), Salamis (480) and Plataea (479). How it declined or fell # The Peloponnesian War (431–404 BCE) between Athens and Sparta exhausted Greece, and Philip II of Macedon won control at Chaeronea (338 BCE). Legacy # Democracy, philosophy (Socrates, Plato, Aristotle), history (Herodotus, Thucydides), theatre and science.

d: Reached the Beas River in Punjab (326 BCE).
x: Overview # Reached the Beas River in Punjab (326 BCE). Government and society # Alexander ruled as king of Macedon and as successor of the Persian Great King, keeping satrapies and mixing Macedonian and Persian officials. How people lived # Soldiers and settlers across new cities. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Hellenistic art and libraries. Food # Greek foods spread across the east; Alexander’s troops encountered sugarcane (‘honey without bees’) in India. Construction and architecture # Alexander founded over a dozen cities called Alexandria, and his successors built the Library and Lighthouse of Alexandria. Technology and knowledge # The sarissa phalanx combined with heavy cavalry, plus siege towers and torsion catapults. How it rose # Philip II reformed the army and unified Greece. Alexander (r. 336–323 BCE) conquered Persia, Egypt and lands to the Indus in 11 years. How it declined or fell # Alexander died in Babylon in 323 BCE at 32. His generals (the Diadochi) split the empire into the Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid kingdoms. Legacy # The Hellenistic age spread Greek language and culture from Egypt to India, including Gandhara art.

d: Conquered the Mediterranean; ended with Julius Caesar and Augustus.
x: Overview # Conquered the Mediterranean; ended with Julius Caesar and Augustus. Government and society # Two consuls elected annually, a Senate of ex-magistrates, and assemblies of citizens. Tribunes protected plebeians, and laws were written on the Twelve Tables (451 BCE). How people lived # Patricians, plebeians and enslaved people Culture, beliefs and heritage # Roman law and festivals like Saturnalia. Food # Puls (wheat porridge), bread, olives, cheese and vegetables; garum fish sauce. Construction and architecture # Roads such as the Via Appia (312 BCE), aqueducts, basilicas and the Forum. Technology and knowledge # Roman concrete, legionary organisation and surveying. How it rose # Romans expelled their last king in 509 BCE, conquered Italy, defeated Carthage and took Greece. How it declined or fell # Inequality, the Gracchi reforms and their murder, generals’ private armies, civil wars from Marius and Sulla to Caesar, and Caesar’s assassination (44 BCE). Octavian became Augustus in 27 BCE. Legacy # Checks and balances, the Senate and republican ideals that inspired the US and French founders.

d: The Western Empire fell in 476 CE; the Eastern lasted to 1453.
x: Overview # The Western Empire fell in 476 CE; the Eastern lasted to 1453. Government and society # Augustus kept the outward forms of the Republic (Senate, consuls) but held real power as princeps, ‘first citizen’, commanding the army and controlling key provinces. The empire was divided into provinces governed by senators or imperial appointees. Roman law developed into a sophisticated system, and citizenship expanded until in 212 CE the emperor Caracalla granted it to nearly all free inhabitants. Society divided into senators, equestrians, citizens, freedmen and enslaved people. How people lived # City dwellers in insulae, peasants and enslaved workers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Baths, games, Latin literature. Food # Bread was so central that the state distributed free grain (the annona) to about 200,000 Roman citizens; Egyptian grain fleets fed the capital. Wealthy Romans dined reclining on dormice, oysters and peacock, recorded in Apicius’ cookbook. Construction and architecture # Romans perfected the arch, vault and dome using concrete: the Pantheon (~125 CE) still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome. They built the Colosseum (seating ~50,000), aqueducts like the Pont du Gard, baths, basilicas, triumphal arches, theatres, apartment blocks (insulae) and planned colonial towns with grid streets, forums and sewers like the Cloaca Maxima. Technology and knowledge # Roman engineers built over 80,000 km of paved roads, aqueducts carrying water by gravity over long distances, hydraulic mining, water mills, cranes powered by treadwheels, underfloor heating (hypocausts), glass-blowing, and concrete using volcanic ash that self-heals in seawater. Medicine advanced under Galen, and the Julian calendar (46 BCE) was a lasting reform. How it rose # Rome grew from a city-state to master of Italy and then the Mediterranean through disciplined citizen legions, alliances, colonies and road-building. After a century of civil wars ended with Octavian’s victory at Actium (31 BCE), the Senate granted him the title Augustus (27 BCE), beginning the Empire. Expansion continued until Trajan’s reign (117 CE). How it declined or fell # The Western Empire weakened over centuries: the Crisis of the Third Century (235–284) brought civil wars, plague, invasions and inflation; Diocletian divided the empire; and it was formally split in 395. Pressure from Germanic peoples displaced by the Huns, the Visigoths’ sack of Rome (410), the Vandals’ seizure of North Africa’s grain (439) and their sack of Rome (455) left the West unable to pay its armies. In 476 the Germanic general Odoacer deposed Romulus Augustulus. The Eastern Empire continued until 1453. Legacy # Roman law underlies many legal systems; Latin gave rise to the Romance languages and much scientific vocabulary; Christianity spread through the empire; and Roman architecture, engineering, the calendar and ideas of citizenship shaped Europe and beyond.

d: Fell to the Ottomans in 1453.
x: Overview # Fell to the Ottomans in 1453. Government and society # An autocratic Christian empire: the emperor was God’s representative, aided by a large salaried bureaucracy. Justinian’s Code (529–534) compiled Roman law. How people lived # Farmers, monks and urban traders. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Icons, mosaics and chariot races. Food # Bread, fish, olive oil, cheese, wine and fasting foods for Orthodox fasts. Construction and architecture # Hagia Sophia (537), whose dome seemed to float on light, Ravenna’s mosaics and the Theodosian Walls of Constantinople. Technology and knowledge # Greek fire, a liquid incendiary weapon, defended the capital, which also had silk production and the gold solidus, a stable coin for 700 years. How it rose # Constantine founded Constantinople in 330. When the Western Empire fell (476), the East continued as the Roman Empire. How it declined or fell # Defeats by Seljuks at Manzikert (1071), the Fourth Crusade’s sack of Constantinople (1204), shrinking territory, and the Ottoman conquest of 1453. Legacy # Preserved Greek and Roman texts, spread Orthodox Christianity and the Cyrillic alphabet to Slavs.

d: Conquered by Rome except in Ireland and northern Britain.
x: Overview # Conquered by Rome except in Ireland and northern Britain. Government and society # Tribes led by chiefs and warrior aristocracies, with druids as priests, judges and teachers. How people lived # Tribal farmers and warriors. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Druidic rituals and La Tène art. Food # Wheat, barley, pork, beer and mead. Construction and architecture # Hillforts, oppida (fortified towns) such as Bibracte, and crannogs (lake dwellings). Technology and knowledge # Iron working, chain mail and fine La Tène metalwork. How it rose # Hallstatt (from ~800 BCE) and La Tène (from ~450 BCE) cultures spread across Europe from Ireland to Anatolia. How it declined or fell # Roman conquest of Gaul (Caesar, 58–50 BCE) and Britain (43 CE); later Germanic migrations. Legacy # Irish, Scottish Gaelic, Welsh and Breton languages and Celtic art.

d: Reached North America ~1000 CE.
x: Overview # Reached North America ~1000 CE. Government and society # Norse chieftains and kings ruled with the advice of the ‘thing’, an assembly of free men. Iceland’s Althing (930) is one of the oldest parliaments. How people lived # Farmers, sailors and traders. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Sagas, runes and the thing assembly. Food # Porridge, bread, dried fish, meat and dairy; ale and mead. Construction and architecture # Longhouses, ring fortresses such as Trelleborg, and stave churches. Technology and knowledge # Clinker-built longships, navigation, and a runic alphabet. How it rose # The raid on Lindisfarne (793) began the Viking Age. They settled in England, Ireland, Normandy, Iceland and Greenland, and reached Newfoundland (~1000). How it declined or fell # Christianisation and stronger kingdoms ended raiding by about 1066. Legacy # Normandy, Kievan Rus, the sagas and many English words.

d: 'Neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire' — Voltaire.
x: Overview # ‘Neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire’ — Voltaire. Government and society # An elected emperor (chosen by seven, later more, prince-electors) presided over hundreds of semi-independent states, cities and bishoprics, with an Imperial Diet (Reichstag). How people lived # Peasants under lords; free cities of merchants. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Gothic cathedrals and printing. Food # Bread, beer, cabbage and pork. Construction and architecture # Aachen Cathedral, Speyer Cathedral and Gothic cathedrals. Technology and knowledge # Gutenberg’s printing press at Mainz (~1450). How it rose # Otto I was crowned emperor in 962, building on Charlemagne’s title (800). How it declined or fell # The Reformation and the Thirty Years’ War (1618–48) weakened it. Napoleon forced its dissolution in 1806. Legacy # German federalism, as Voltaire mocked: ‘neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire’.

d: Destroyed by the Mongols.
x: Overview # Destroyed by the Mongols. Government and society # Rurikid princes ruled Kiev and other cities with councils of nobles (boyars) and town assemblies (veche). How people lived # Trade on the river route to Byzantium Culture, beliefs and heritage # Orthodox icons and onion domes. Food # Rye bread, kasha and kvass. Construction and architecture # St Sophia’s Cathedral in Kyiv and the Golden Gate. Technology and knowledge # Trade along the Dnieper to Byzantium. How it rose # Varangian (Viking) leader Rurik and his successor Oleg united eastern Slav lands in the late 9th century. How it declined or fell # Princely feuds and the Mongol destruction of Kyiv (1240). Legacy # Christianisation by Vladimir (988); shared heritage of Ukraine, Belarus and Russia.

d: 'The empire on which the sun never sets' (first).
x: Overview # ‘The empire on which the sun never sets’ (first). Government and society # The Habsburg monarchy ruled through councils (the Council of the Indies) and viceroyalties of New Spain and Peru. How people lived # Colonists, Indigenous labourers and enslaved Africans. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Baroque churches and mestizo culture. Food # The Columbian Exchange brought maize, potatoes, tomatoes and chocolate to Europe and wheat and cattle to the Americas. Construction and architecture # Baroque cathedrals and colonial grid towns across the Americas, and El Escorial. Technology and knowledge # Silver mining at Potosí using mercury amalgamation; Manila galleons crossing the Pacific. How it rose # Columbus’s voyage (1492), conquest of the Aztecs (1521) and Incas (1532). How it declined or fell # Wars, inflation, then independence movements (1810–1825) in Latin America and defeat by the US (1898). Legacy # Spanish is spoken by about 500 million people; the Columbian Exchange.

d: Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498.
x: Overview # Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. Government and society # Crown-sponsored trading posts (feitorias) and captaincies. How people lived # Sailors, traders and colonists. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Azulejo tiles and Indo-Portuguese culture in Goa. Food # Spice trade; chillies brought from America to India. Construction and architecture # Forts in Goa, Malacca and Africa; the Manueline style. Technology and knowledge # Caravels and astronomical navigation. How it rose # Henry the Navigator’s voyages; Vasco da Gama reached India in 1498. How it declined or fell # Dutch competition, Brazilian independence (1822), and African wars of independence after 1974. Legacy # The Portuguese language and Goan culture.

d: India was its most valuable colony.
x: Overview # India was its most valuable colony. Government and society # Colonies ranged from self-governing dominions to crown colonies and princely states, overseen from London. How people lived # Settlers, colonial subjects and indentured labourers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Cricket, the English language and global sport. Food # Tea, sugar and spices were traded; slave plantations produced sugar. Construction and architecture # Colonial capitals such as New Delhi and Indo-Saracenic railway stations. Technology and knowledge # Steamships, railways and the telegraph. How it rose # Atlantic colonies, East India Company conquests in India, and industrial and naval power. How it declined or fell # World wars, independence movements (India 1947), and decolonisation by the 1960s. Legacy # English as a world language and the Commonwealth, but also exploitation, famines and partitions.

d: Ended in the 1917 revolution.
x: Overview # Ended in the 1917 revolution. Government and society # An autocratic tsar ruled with the nobility and Orthodox Church; serfdom lasted until 1861. How people lived # Serfs, nobles and merchants. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Tolstoy, Tchaikovsky and Orthodox festivals. Food # Rye bread, cabbage soup (shchi) and kasha. Construction and architecture # St Petersburg, Peter the Great’s ‘window to the West’. Technology and knowledge # Trans-Siberian railway. How it rose # Peter the Great proclaimed the empire in 1721 and it expanded across Siberia to the Pacific. How it declined or fell # Defeat by Japan (1905), World War I losses, and the 1917 revolutions. Legacy # Tolstoy, Dostoevsky, Tchaikovsky.

d: Dissolved into 15 states in 1991.
x: Overview # Dissolved into 15 states in 1991. Government and society # A one-party Communist state with a centrally planned economy. How people lived # Collective farmers and industrial workers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Constructivist art, ballet and space-age culture. Food # Bread, potatoes and cabbage; famines in 1932–33 killed millions. Construction and architecture # Stalinist ‘Seven Sisters’ skyscrapers. Technology and knowledge # Sputnik (1957), Gagarin (1961) and nuclear weapons. How it rose # The Bolshevik revolution (1917) and the civil war. How it declined or fell # Economic stagnation, Afghanistan, nationalism and Gorbachev’s reforms led to dissolution in 1991. Legacy # The defeat of Nazism at huge cost; Cold War; Stalin’s terror and famines.

d: Contemporaneous with Egypt's pyramids.
x: Overview # Contemporaneous with Egypt’s pyramids. Government and society # There is no evidence of warfare. Elites probably organised large labour projects and trade between coast and valley. How people lived # Pyramid towns trading cotton and fish Culture, beliefs and heritage # Flutes and ceremonial plazas. Food # Anchovies and sardines from the coast traded for squash, beans and cotton. Construction and architecture # Caral’s stepped pyramids and sunken circular plazas, built around 2600 BCE, as old as Egypt’s pyramids. Technology and knowledge # Cotton fishing nets, irrigation and quipu-like knotted cords. How it rose # Fishing and cotton farming supported about 30 centres in Peru’s Supe valley from around 3000 BCE. How it declined or fell # Climate shifts and El Niño events led to decline around 1800 BCE. Legacy # The oldest civilisation of the Americas.

d: The 'mother culture' of Mesoamerica.
x: Overview # The ‘mother culture’ of Mesoamerica. Government and society # Rulers depicted as divine are commemorated in colossal stone heads. How people lived # Farmers and ceremonial centres. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Jaguar imagery and the ballgame. Food # Maize processed with lime (nixtamalisation), beans and squash. Construction and architecture # La Venta’s earthen pyramid and San Lorenzo’s plaza. Technology and knowledge # Rubber (from which their Aztec name derives) and possibly the first Mesoamerican writing and calendar. How it rose # Emerged on the Gulf Coast of Mexico around 1500 BCE. How it declined or fell # Abandoned by about 400 BCE, possibly due to river changes. Legacy # Often called the ‘mother culture’ of Mesoamerica.

d: Classic cities declined amid drought and war around 800–900 CE.
x: Overview # Classic cities declined amid drought and war around 800–900 CE. Government and society # Dozens of city-states were ruled by divine kings (k’uhul ajaw). Rivals like Tikal and Calakmul fought long wars. How people lived # Maize farmers in villages around temple cities. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The ballgame, glyph writing and the Popol Vuh. Food # Maize was sacred; people ate tortillas, tamales and atole, with beans, squash, chilli and turkey. Elites drank frothy cacao. Construction and architecture # Pyramid temples at Tikal, Palenque, Copán and Chichén Itzá; ball courts and causeways. Lidar has revealed huge networks of farms and roads. Technology and knowledge # A full writing system, the concept of zero, the Long Count calendar and precise astronomy (the Dresden Codex Venus tables). How it rose # Villages from about 2000 BCE became cities such as El Mirador in the Preclassic period. How it declined or fell # Classic southern cities were abandoned around 800–950 CE after droughts, warfare and overpopulation. Northern cities and highland kingdoms lasted until Spanish conquest (the last, Nojpetén, fell in 1697). Legacy # Over six million Maya people today still speak about 30 Maya languages.

d: Its name means 'place where the gods were created'.
x: Overview # Its name means ‘place where the gods were created’. Government and society # A city with possibly collective rule, as few royal images are known. How people lived # Craftsmen and farmers in apartment compounds. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Feathered serpent imagery. Food # Maize, beans, squash, amaranth and pulque. Construction and architecture # The Pyramid of the Sun, the Pyramid of the Moon and the Avenue of the Dead, laid out on a grid. Technology and knowledge # Obsidian workshops and apartment compounds for about 100,000 people. How it rose # Grew from about 100 BCE. How it declined or fell # Its centre burned around 550 CE, perhaps in internal revolt. Legacy # The Aztecs named it ‘place where gods were born’.

d: Tenochtitlan (~200,000) fell to Cortés and smallpox.
x: Overview # Tenochtitlan (~200,000) fell to Cortés and smallpox. Government and society # The Triple Alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan collected tribute from conquered city-states. The huey tlatoani was elected by a council of nobles. How people lived # Calpulli neighbourhoods of farmers and artisans. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Feathered art, poetry and markets like Tlatelolco. Food # Maize tortillas, beans, squash, chilli, amaranth and chinampa vegetables; nobles drank chocolate. Construction and architecture # Tenochtitlan, an island city of perhaps 200,000 people with causeways, aqueducts, the Templo Mayor and chinampa floating gardens. Technology and knowledge # Chinampa agriculture, the 365-day and 260-day calendars, and universal schooling for boys. How it rose # The Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 and the Triple Alliance formed in 1428. How it declined or fell # Hernán Cortés, with tens of thousands of indigenous allies and a smallpox epidemic, besieged Tenochtitlan until it fell in 1521. Legacy # Mexico’s flag, the Nahuatl language (chocolate, tomato, avocado).

d: The largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas.
x: Overview # The largest empire in the pre-Columbian Americas. Government and society # The Sapa Inca ruled Tawantinsuyu, the ‘four parts together’, through provincial governors. Labour tax (mit’a) built roads and storehouses. How people lived # Ayllu kin groups of farmers owing labour (mit’a). Culture, beliefs and heritage # Inti Raymi and fine textiles. Food # Potatoes (freeze-dried as chuño), maize, quinoa and llama meat; storehouses (qollqa) held food for years. Construction and architecture # Machu Picchu, Sacsayhuamán with its precisely fitted stones, and Cusco. Technology and knowledge # About 40,000 km of roads with rope bridges, quipu knot records, freeze-dried food (chuño) and terrace farming. How it rose # Pachacuti (r. 1438–1471) turned the Cusco kingdom into an empire. How it declined or fell # Smallpox, a civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa, and Pizarro’s capture of Atahualpa at Cajamarca (1532). Legacy # Quechua spoken by about 8 million people; the potato.

d: Abandoned many sites during the great drought of 1276–99.
x: Overview # Abandoned many sites during the great drought of 1276–99. Government and society # Clan-based villages with religious leaders. How people lived # Dry farming with irrigation Culture, beliefs and heritage # Kivas and pottery. Food # Maize, beans and squash, plus wild game. Construction and architecture # Pueblo Bonito at Chaco Canyon and Mesa Verde’s cliff dwellings. Technology and knowledge # Roads aligned with astronomy and water management. How it rose # From about 750 CE in the US Southwest. How it declined or fell # Great Drought (1276–1299) and conflict led to migration. Legacy # Hopi, Zuni and other Pueblo peoples.

d: Monks Mound is the largest pre-Columbian earthwork north of Mexico.
x: Overview # Monks Mound is the largest pre-Columbian earthwork north of Mexico. Government and society # Chiefdoms ruled by paramount chiefs. How people lived # Maize farmers around mound centres. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Shell gorgets and ceremonial mounds. Food # Maize, beans and squash. Construction and architecture # Cahokia’s Monks Mound, the largest earthwork in North America. Technology and knowledge # Maize farming. How it rose # Cahokia grew rapidly around 1050 CE. How it declined or fell # Floods, drought and political change; Cahokia was abandoned by 1350. Legacy # The largest pre-Columbian city north of Mexico.

d: Influenced debates about American federalism.
x: Overview # Influenced debates about American federalism. Government and society # The Great Law of Peace united five (later six) nations with a council of chiefs chosen by clan mothers. How people lived # Longhouse families led by clan mothers. Culture, beliefs and heritage # The Great Law of Peace and wampum belts. Food # The Three Sisters: maize, beans and squash planted together. Construction and architecture # Longhouses. Technology and knowledge # The Three Sisters (maize, beans, squash) and wampum belts. How it rose # Founded by Deganawida and Hiawatha (dates debated from 1142 to around 1450). How it declined or fell # Wars and land loss after the American Revolution. Legacy # Possibly influenced US federalism.

d: Became the leading world power after 1945.
x: Overview # Became the leading world power after 1945. Government and society # A federal constitutional republic with separation of powers and a Bill of Rights. How people lived # Farmers, industrial workers and later a service economy. Culture, beliefs and heritage # Jazz, Hollywood and the internet. Food # Corn, wheat and beef; fast food spread worldwide in the 20th century. Construction and architecture # The Capitol and skyscrapers. Technology and knowledge # The telephone, aeroplane, atomic bomb, the Moon landing and the internet. How it rose # Independence (1776), westward expansion and industrialisation. How it declined or fell # Still in existence. Legacy # A superpower since 1945.

How it rose to power # Bimbisara (r. c. 544–492 BCE) built Magadha’s power by marriage alliances with Kosala, the Licchavis and Madra, and by annexing Anga, which gave him the port of Champa and Ganga trade. He organised officials to collect land revenue directly. His son Ajatashatru fought a long war against the Vajji confederacy, reportedly using new weapons such as a catapult and a scythed chariot, and fortified the village of Pataligrama, later Pataliputra. How it lost power # Haryanka kings are remembered in Buddhist texts as patricides: Ajatashatru is said to have killed Bimbisara, and his successors killed their fathers in turn. Disgusted, the people and ministers deposed the last Haryanka king, Nagadasaka, and raised the minister Shishunaga to the throne around 413 BCE.

How it rose to power # Mahapadma Nanda, said by Puranas to be the son of a Shudra woman, overthrew the Shishunagas and defeated many older kshatriya dynasties, earning the title ‘destroyer of all kshatriyas’. The Nandas built the first huge standing army in India — Greek sources speak of 200,000 infantry, 20,000 cavalry, 2,000 chariots and 3,000–6,000 elephants — which deterred Alexander’s tired troops from crossing the Beas in 326 BCE. How it lost power # Heavy taxation and the low-born status ascribed to them made the Nandas unpopular. Tradition says the Brahmin Chanakya, insulted at Dhana Nanda’s court, trained the young Chandragupta Maurya, who raised an army in the northwest and overthrew Dhana Nanda around 322 BCE.

How it rose to power # Chandragupta Maurya, advised by the Brahmin strategist Chanakya, overthrew the unpopular Nanda dynasty of Magadha around 322 BCE, after Alexander’s withdrawal from Punjab left a power vacuum in the northwest. In about 303 BCE he defeated or made peace with Seleucus I, gaining Afghanistan and Baluchistan in exchange for 500 war elephants. His son Bindusara expanded into the Deccan, and Ashoka conquered Kalinga (261 BCE), bringing almost the whole subcontinent except the far south under one rule. How it lost power # After Ashoka’s death in 232 BCE the empire split between successors, provinces broke away, and revenue fell. Some historians blame the costs of a vast bureaucracy and army; others cite Ashoka’s pacifism weakening the military, though this is disputed. In 185 BCE the general Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated the last Mauryan king, Brihadratha, during an army review and founded the Shunga dynasty, while Indo-Greeks invaded from the northwest.

How it rose to power # In about 185 BCE the commander-in-chief Pushyamitra Shunga assassinated the last Maurya emperor, Brihadratha, during a military parade and took the throne. He performed Vedic horse sacrifices (ashvamedha) to proclaim sovereignty and fought off Indo-Greek raids; his grandson Vasumitra defeated Greeks on the Sindhu river. How it lost power # The Shunga realm shrank to Magadha and central India (Vidisha). Its last king Devabhuti was killed in a palace plot by his minister Vasudeva Kanva around 73 BCE, who founded the short-lived Kanva dynasty. Shunga-era art survives on the Bharhut stupa and the Sanchi gateways’ early phases.

d: 200 BCE–10 CE
x: How it rose to power # Greek kingdoms of Bactria, left over from Alexander’s conquest and the Seleucid empire, crossed the Hindu Kush around 200 BCE under Demetrius I as Mauryan power faded. Menander I (Milinda, r. c. 165–130 BCE) ruled from Sagala (Sialkot) and is remembered in the Buddhist Milindapanha dialogue with the monk Nagasena. How it lost power # The Indo-Greeks fragmented into some 30 rival kings and were squeezed by Scythians (Sakas), Parthians and finally the Kushans; the last ruler, Strato II, disappears around 10 CE. They left bilingual Greek–Kharosthi coins with realistic portraits and contributed to Gandhara art.

d: c. 100 BCE–220 CE
x: How it rose to power # After the Mauryas declined, Simuka founded the dynasty around the 1st century BCE in the western Deccan. How it lost power # Wars with the Western Kshatrapas and internal division split the realm into smaller kingdoms by the early 3rd century.

How it rose to power # Saka (Scythian) governors who had served the Kushans established themselves in Gujarat, Malwa and Saurashtra in the 1st century CE. Rudradaman I (r. c. 130–150) defeated the Satavahanas twice and left the Junagadh rock inscription (150 CE) — the earliest long inscription in Sanskrit — recording repairs to the Mauryan Sudarshana lake. How it lost power # Gupta emperor Chandragupta II conquered them around 395–415 CE, gaining the rich ports of western India; legend links this victory to the hero Vikramaditya. Their dated coins are a key source for Indian chronology.

How it rose to power # The Guptas began as a minor family in Magadha. Chandragupta I (r. ~320–335) married Kumaradevi, a princess of the powerful Licchavi clan, which raised his status. His son Samudragupta (r. ~335–375), celebrated in the Allahabad pillar inscription, conquered or subdued kings across northern India and received tribute from the south. Chandragupta II (r. ~375–415) defeated the Western Kshatrapas, gaining Gujarat’s sea trade. How it lost power # From around 460 CE the Alchon Huns (Hunas) invaded from Central Asia. Skandagupta repelled them at first, but later attacks under Toramana and Mihirakula devastated the northwest and drained the treasury. At the same time feudatories such as the Maukharis and Maitrakas became independent, trade with the Roman world declined, and the dynasty faded by around 550.

How it rose to power # Founded by Vindhyashakti around 250 CE in the Deccan after the Satavahanas collapsed, the Vakatakas performed Vedic sacrifices and ruled central India. Chandragupta II married his daughter Prabhavatigupta to the Vakataka king; as regent she ruled for years, binding the two dynasties. How it lost power # The kingdom split into two branches, which declined in the late 5th century under pressure from neighbours such as the Vishnukundins and Kalachuris. Their great legacy is the later Ajanta caves, sponsored under King Harishena (r. c. 460–478).

How it rose to power # The Pushyabhutis ruled Thanesar (Haryana) and rose by fighting the Hunas. Harshavardhana (r. 606–647) took over Kannauj after his sister’s husband was killed, uniting most of north India. Xuanzang described his huge assemblies at Prayag, where Harsha gave away all his wealth every five years. How it lost power # Harsha was defeated by Pulakeshin II on the Narmada (c. 618) and left no heir; after his death in 647 a minister usurped the throne and the empire disintegrated. Kannauj became the prize fought over by Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas.

How it rose to power # Nagabhata I (c. 730–760) won fame by repelling Arab armies from Sindh, protecting western India. His successors took Kannauj (c. 816) and under Mihira Bhoja (r. 836–885) ruled from Gujarat to Bengal; the Arab traveller Sulaiman called them hostile to Islam but praised their security. How it lost power # A century of tripartite struggle with Palas and Rashtrakutas exhausted them; Rashtrakuta Indra III sacked Kannauj in 916. Mahmud of Ghazni’s raid in 1018 broke them, and smaller Rajput clans (Chandela, Paramara, Chauhan) succeeded.

How it rose to power # Gopala’s election around 750; Dharmapala and Devapala expanded the realm across north India. How it lost power # Weakened by Pratihara and Rashtrakuta wars, they were overthrown by the Senas in the 12th century.

How it rose to power # Dantidurga, a Chalukya feudatory, overthrew Kirtivarman II around 753 and founded the Rashtrakuta dynasty in the Deccan. His successor Krishna I commissioned the monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora. Dhruva and Govinda III raided as far as Kannauj, and Amoghavarsha I (r. 814–878), who reigned 64 years, founded the capital Manyakheta and wrote the Kannada poetics work Kavirajamarga. How it lost power # Their wars with Pratiharas, Palas, Cholas and Eastern Chalukyas were endless. Krishna III won a great victory over the Cholas at Takkolam (949), but soon after Paramara king Siyaka sacked Manyakheta (972). A feudatory, Tailapa II, overthrew the last Rashtrakuta king in 973, founding the Western Chalukyas of Kalyani.

How it rose to power # The early Cholas appear in Sangam literature, but the Imperial Cholas began when Vijayalaya captured Thanjavur from the Muttaraiyars around 848. Rajaraja I (985–1014) conquered the Cheras, Pandyas, northern Sri Lanka and the Maldives; his son Rajendra I (1014–1044) marched to the Ganga, founding Gangaikonda Cholapuram (‘city of the Chola who conquered the Ganga’), and sent a naval expedition against the Srivijaya empire in 1025. How it lost power # Long wars with the Western Chalukyas drained resources. In the 12th–13th centuries, provincial chiefs grew powerful, the Pandyas revived in the south and the Hoysalas in the west. The last Chola king, Rajendra III, was defeated by the Pandya Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan around 1279.

How it rose to power # Tailapa II, a Rashtrakuta feudatory claiming Chalukya descent, overthrew his overlords in 973 and ruled from Kalyani. His dynasty fought long wars with the Cholas over the Raichur doab. Vikramaditya VI (r. 1076–1126) started his own era and patronised the poet Bilhana and jurist Vijnaneshwara, author of the Mitakshara law commentary. How it lost power # Feudatories grew powerful — the Kalachuris seized Kalyani in 1157, and Hoysalas, Yadavas and Kakatiyas divided the realm by 1189. Their ornate temples in Lakkundi and Itagi developed the Kalyani Chalukya style.

How it rose to power # Hill chiefs from the Malnad region of Karnataka, the Hoysalas served as Chalukya feudatories and became independent under Vishnuvardhana (r. 1108–1152), who reportedly converted from Jainism to Vaishnavism under Ramanuja. How it lost power # They were caught between Pandyas and Yadavas, and the Delhi Sultanate’s general Malik Kafur sacked their capital Dwarasamudra in 1311. Veera Ballala III died fighting the Madurai Sultanate in 1343; his officers Harihara and Bukka helped found Vijayanagara. Their star-shaped temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are UNESCO-listed.

How it rose to power # Kakatiyas were Chalukya feudatories in Telangana who became independent under Prola II and Rudra I (c. 1163). Ganapati (r. 1199–1262) and his daughter Rudramadevi, one of India’s few reigning queens, built Warangal fort and the Thousand Pillar and Ramappa temples, and an irrigation system of tanks. How it lost power # The Delhi Sultanate attacked repeatedly; Muhammad bin Tughlaq (then Ulugh Khan) captured Warangal in 1323 and took Prataparudra prisoner. The Kakatiya tanks and Ramappa temple (UNESCO 2021) remain.

How it rose to power # Anantavarman Chodaganga (r. 1078–1147) ruled from the Godavari to the Ganga and began the Jagannath temple at Puri. Narasimhadeva I (r. 1238–1264) defeated Bengal’s Muslim rulers and built the Sun Temple at Konark, conceived as a giant stone chariot with 24 wheels. How it lost power # Weakened by Delhi and Bengal sultanates and internal revolts, the last Ganga king was overthrown in 1434 by his minister Kapilendra Deva, founder of the Gajapati dynasty.

How it rose to power # Qutb ud-Din Aibak, a Turkic slave who rose as Muhammad of Ghor’s general, ruled from Delhi from 1206. Iltutmish (r. 1211–1236) consolidated the Sultanate, received caliphal recognition and introduced silver tanka and copper jital coins; his daughter Razia (r. 1236–40) was the only woman to rule Delhi. Balban (r. 1266–87) held off the Mongols with harsh rule. How it lost power # After Balban’s death his weak grandson Kaiqubad was killed, and the Khalji nobles took power in 1290.

How it rose to power # Jalaluddin Khalji seized power in 1290, ending the Turkish nobles’ monopoly. His nephew Alauddin murdered him in 1296 and, with the loot of Devagiri, made himself sultan. Alauddin defeated several Mongol invasions, introduced market price controls, and sent Malik Kafur on raids to Warangal, Dwarasamudra and Madurai. How it lost power # After Alauddin’s death in 1316, Malik Kafur’s brief regency and the murders of rival princes led to the rise of Khusrau Khan, killed by Ghazi Malik (Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq) in 1320.

How it rose to power # Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded the dynasty in 1320 and built Tughlaqabad. Muhammad bin Tughlaq (r. 1325–51) was brilliant but erratic: token currency, a move of capital to Daulatabad and a planned conquest of Khurasan all failed. Firuz Shah (r. 1351–88) built canals, towns and hospitals. How it lost power # Revolts produced the Bahmani Sultanate and Vijayanagara (1336–47). Timur sacked Delhi in 1398, killing tens of thousands; the dynasty limped on until 1414.

How it rose to power # Bahlul Lodi, an Afghan governor, took the throne in 1451. Sikandar Lodi (r. 1489–1517) founded Agra and made it his capital. How it lost power # Ibrahim Lodi alienated Afghan nobles, who invited Babur from Kabul. Babur’s field guns and tactics defeated him at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

How it rose to power # Founded in 1347 by Alauddin Bahman Shah, who rebelled against Muhammad bin Tughlaq, with capitals at Gulbarga and Bidar. Minister Mahmud Gawan reformed administration and built a madrasa in Bidar. How it lost power # Factional conflict between Deccani and foreign nobles, and Gawan’s execution in 1481, led to five successor sultanates: Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Berar and Bidar.

How it rose to power # Brothers Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama family founded the empire in 1336 to resist the Delhi Sultanate’s raids into the south. How it lost power # An alliance of the Deccan sultanates defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565; Hampi was sacked for months. The dynasty continued weakly until 1646.

How it rose to power # Babur, a Timurid prince from Fergana descended from both Timur and Genghis Khan, invaded India and defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526) and Rana Sanga at Khanwa (1527). His son Humayun lost the empire to Sher Shah Suri (1540) and regained it in 1555. Akbar (r. 1556–1605) won the Second Battle of Panipat and built a stable empire through conquest, alliances and reforms. How it lost power # Aurangzeb (r. 1658–1707) expanded the empire to its largest extent but spent 25 years at war in the Deccan against the Marathas, emptying the treasury, while reimposing the jizya alienated many subjects. After his death, wars of succession, rebellious governors (Bengal, Awadh, Hyderabad), Maratha expansion, Sikh and Jat revolts, Nadir Shah’s devastating sack of Delhi (1739) and Afghan invasions shattered central power. The East India Company reduced the emperors to pensioners, and the last emperor, Bahadur Shah Zafar, was exiled after 1857.

How it rose to power # Sher Shah Suri, an Afghan commander, defeated the Mughal Humayun at Chausa (1539) and Kannauj (1540) and ruled north India. He introduced the silver rupiya, land measurement, and rebuilt the Grand Trunk Road with caravanserais. How it lost power # Sher Shah died in a gunpowder explosion in 1545. Succession quarrels let Humayun return; Akbar’s general defeated Hemu at the Second Battle of Panipat (1556).

How it rose to power # Hammir Singh recaptured Chittor around 1326 after Alauddin Khalji’s siege of 1303. Rana Kumbha (r. 1433–68) built the Vijay Stambh and Kumbhalgarh fort; Rana Sanga united Rajputs against Babur. How it lost power # Mewar never fully submitted: Maharana Pratap fought Akbar at Haldighati (1576). It accepted Mughal suzerainty in 1615 and British protection in 1818, and merged into India in 1948.

How it rose to power # The Tai prince Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills in 1228 and united local peoples. How it lost power # Civil war, Burmese invasions (1817–1826) and British annexation after the Treaty of Yandabo (1826).

How it rose to power # Shivaji (1630–1680) built a state in the Western Ghats by seizing Bijapur forts, defeated Afzal Khan (1659), escaped from Aurangzeb’s custody at Agra (1666) and was crowned Chhatrapati in 1674. After Aurangzeb’s death the Marathas expanded across India under Peshwa Bajirao I. How it lost power # Defeat by Ahmad Shah Durrani at the Third Battle of Panipat (1761) cost a generation of leaders. Internal rivalries let the British win three Anglo-Maratha Wars; the confederacy ended in 1818.

How it rose to power # Ranjit Singh unified the Sikh misls and captured Lahore in 1799, then Multan, Kashmir and Peshawar. How it lost power # After his death in 1839, court intrigue and assassinations weakened the state; the British won the Anglo-Sikh Wars (1845–46, 1848–49) and annexed Punjab.

How it rose to power # Hyder Ali seized power from the Wodeyars and expanded Mysore across the south. How it lost power # Four Anglo-Mysore Wars; Tipu died defending Srirangapatna in 1799, and the British restored the Wodeyars as subordinate rulers.

How it rose to power # Asaf Jah I, the Mughal viceroy of the Deccan, became independent in 1724. Later Nizams allied with the British as a ‘subsidiary’ state. How it lost power # The last Nizam, Osman Ali Khan, one of the world’s richest men, refused to join India; Operation Polo (1948) integrated Hyderabad.

How it rose to power # Cyrus the Great overthrew the Medes (550 BCE), conquered Lydia and Babylon (539 BCE), and his successors took Egypt and northwest India. How it lost power # Costly wars with Greece, palace intrigue and revolts weakened it; Alexander defeated Darius III at Issus and Gaugamela (331 BCE).

How it rose to power # Seleucus I, Alexander’s general, took Babylon in 312 BCE and built an empire from Anatolia to Bactria; he traded India’s eastern provinces to Chandragupta for 500 elephants. Antioch became a great city. How it lost power # Parthians and Bactrians broke away; Rome defeated Antiochus III at Magnesia (190 BCE). Pompey annexed Syria in 63 BCE.

d: 247 BCE–224 CE
x: How it rose to power # Arsaces I led the Parni nomads to seize Parthia around 247 BCE; Mithridates I conquered Mesopotamia. Parthian horse archers destroyed a Roman army at Carrhae (53 BCE). How it lost power # Repeated Roman invasions and civil wars weakened them; their vassal Ardashir I of Persis killed the last king in 224 CE.

How it rose to power # Ardashir I founded the empire in 224, promoting Zoroastrianism as state religion. Shapur I captured the Roman emperor Valerian (260). Khosrow I (r. 531–579) reformed taxes and welcomed scholars. How it lost power # An exhausting war with Byzantium (602–628) and civil war left them weak against the Arab armies, which won at Qadisiyya (636) and Nahavand (642).

How it rose to power # After Muhammad’s death in 632, Abu Bakr was chosen caliph and reunited Arabia. Umar’s armies conquered Syria, Egypt, Iraq and Persia. How it lost power # Uthman was killed in 656; the first civil war between Ali and Muawiya followed, and Ali was murdered in 661.

How it rose to power # Muawiya founded the Umayyad dynasty in Damascus. Its armies reached Spain (711) and Sindh (712). Abd al-Malik built the Dome of the Rock and made Arabic the administrative language. How it lost power # Non-Arab Muslims resented their status; the Abbasid revolution defeated them on the Zab in 750. An Umayyad prince founded the Emirate of Córdoba.

How it rose to power # Founded on the Abbasid revolution in 750; al-Mansur founded Baghdad in 762. Under Harun al-Rashid and al-Mamun the House of Wisdom translated Greek and Indian works. How it lost power # Provincial dynasties split away, Turkish soldiers took control, and the Mongols under Hulagu sacked Baghdad in 1258.

How it rose to power # Ismaili Shia leader al-Mahdi founded the caliphate in Tunisia (909); they conquered Egypt in 969 and founded Cairo and al-Azhar. How it lost power # Crusades, famine and military feuds; Saladin abolished it in 1171.

How it rose to power # Tughril Beg led Oghuz Turks to take Baghdad in 1055. Alp Arslan defeated Byzantium at Manzikert (1071), opening Anatolia to Turks; vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded madrasas. How it lost power # It fragmented after Malik Shah’s death (1092); the Khwarazmians defeated the last Great Seljuk in 1194.

How it rose to power # Saladin, a Kurdish general, ended the Fatimids, united Egypt and Syria, and recaptured Jerusalem in 1187. How it lost power # Family rivalries; Mamluk soldiers killed the last sultan in 1250.

How it rose to power # Turkic and Circassian slave soldiers (mamluks) killed the last Ayyubid sultan in 1250. They defeated the Mongols at Ain Jalut (1260) under Baybars and expelled the last crusaders (Acre, 1291); Cairo became the Islamic world’s greatest city. How it lost power # Plague, Portuguese disruption of the spice trade and outdated tactics weakened them; Selim I’s Ottoman artillery won at Marj Dabiq (1516) and Ridaniya (1517).

How it rose to power # Hulagu Khan, Genghis Khan’s grandson, destroyed the Assassins’ fortresses and sacked Baghdad (1258), killing the last Abbasid caliph, and founded the Ilkhanate in Persia and Iraq. Ghazan Khan converted to Islam (1295), and his vizier Rashid al-Din wrote the Jami al-Tawarikh, the first world history. How it lost power # The Mamluks stopped Ilkhanid expansion at Ain Jalut (1260). Abu Said died in 1335 without an heir, and the realm split into regional dynasties such as the Jalayirids and Muzaffarids, later swept up by Timur.

How it rose to power # Timur conquered from Delhi to Anatolia and made Samarkand dazzling. His grandson Ulugh Beg built an observatory. How it lost power # Divided among heirs; Uzbeks took Samarkand in 1500–07. Babur founded the Mughal Empire.

How it rose to power # Osman I’s frontier principality in Anatolia expanded into the Balkans; Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453; Selim I took Egypt and Arabia; Suleiman reached Vienna (1529). How it lost power # Military defeats from 1683, nationalism in the Balkans, economic dependence on Europe and defeat in World War I led to its dissolution and the Turkish Republic (1923).

How it rose to power # Ismail I, head of a Sufi order, took Tabriz (1501) and imposed Shia Islam. Shah Abbas I (r. 1588–1629) moved the capital to Isfahan. How it lost power # Weak shahs and the Afghan siege of Isfahan (1722); Nader Shah ended the dynasty in 1736.

How it rose to power # Agha Mohammad Khan, a Turkmen chief, reunited Iran by 1794 and made Tehran his capital. How it lost power # Losses to Russia, concessions to foreigners, the 1906 Constitutional Revolution, and Reza Khan’s coup (1921) led to their deposition in 1925.
